title: TRPV1: the capsaicin and heat receptor
objective: Explain how TRPV1 was identified, what activates it, and what knockout mice revealed about its role.

steps.title: Found by asking 'what does chili bind?'
steps.body:
In 1997 the Julius lab screened a sensory-neuron cDNA library for a gene that would make ordinary cells respond to **[[capsaicin]]**, the compound in chili. The gene encoded **[[TRPV1]]**.

It was also opened by **noxious heat** (above roughly 43 °C) and by **acid**, showing one channel could detect a chemical, a temperature and tissue acidity.

steps.prompt: What did finding TRPV1 explain about eating chili peppers?
options: Capsaicin chemically burns and damages the tissue it touches
Capsaicin opens the same channel heat does, so it reads as burning
Capsaicin activates touch afferents, which the brain misreads as heat
Capsaicin blocks cold receptors, and losing cold feels like heat
steps.explanation: Same channel, same neurons, same 'line' to the brain. Chili feels hot because it activates the heat detector (the labeled-line logic from A1-L4).

variants.setup: Capsaicin and noxious heat both open TRPV1 on the same neurons.
options: Cold, in the way menthol does
Burning heat, because the heat channel is opened
A gentle brushing touch
Nothing in particular
variants.reveal: Activating the heat detector any way reads as heat — the labeled-line logic behind why chili 'burns.'

steps.title: Knockouts: what TRPV1 is needed for
steps.body:
Mice without TRPV1 (2000) ignored capsaicin and had reduced responses to strong heat. Most strikingly, they largely failed to develop **heat hypersensitivity after inflammation**.

So TRPV1 matters most when tissue is inflamed: inflammatory signals sensitize it, lowering its heat threshold so normally warm temperatures begin to hurt (A9).

steps.setup: You inflame a mouse's paw. In wild-type mice, warm (not hot) stimuli now cause withdrawal.
steps.prompt: What do you predict for TRPV1-knockout mice?
options: Same hypersensitivity
Much less heat hypersensitivity
They become cold-sensitive instead
They feel no touch
steps.reveal: The knockout mice largely lack inflammatory heat hypersensitivity, pointing to TRPV1 sensitization as a key mechanism.

flag.note: Knockouts kept some response to strong heat, so other heat detectors also contribute.

variants.prompt: After paw inflammation, wild-type mice become hypersensitive to warmth. TRPV1-knockout mice mostly do not. This shows TRPV1 is…
options: Unrelated to heat sensation
Key to inflammatory heat hypersensitivity
The only heat sensor there is
A channel for touch, not heat
variants.explanation: Losing the inflammatory heat hypersensitivity in the knockout points to TRPV1 sensitization as the mechanism — though some noxious-heat response remains via other sensors.

steps.prompt: Why is TRPV1 a useful genetic handle for reaching many nociceptors?
options: Because TRPV1 is expressed by essentially every neuron in the body
Many nociceptors express TRPV1, so a Trpv1 line can target them
Because TRPV1 is found only in muscle, which gives very clean access
It isn't a useful handle; TRPV1 is never used to target neurons
steps.explanation: TRPV1 marks a broad nociceptor population, which is why Trpv1-Cre lines are common; A3-L4 covers the caveats.

variants.setup: You need genetic access to many nociceptors at once.
variants.prompt: Why is a Trpv1-driven Cre line a reasonable choice?
options: Because TRPV1 is expressed by every neuron in the body
Because a broad set of nociceptors express TRPV1
Because TRPV1 is unique to one colon neuron
Because TRPV1 is never expressed in sensory neurons
variants.reveal: TRPV1 marks a large nociceptor population, handy for access — though the developmental-lineage caveat (A3-L4) still applies.
